extracted.intended_audience: employers, workers, labor lawyers, courts, and regulators evaluating FLSA worker classification
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for determining whether a worker is an employee or an independent contractor under the Fair Labor Standards Act using the economic-reality test; explains factors to consider, relevant case examples, and how to weigh evidence under a totality-of-the-circumstances approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Totality of the circumstances (no single factor dispositive)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determination must employ a totality-of-the-circumstances approach; none of the factors alone is controlling or dispositive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts and the Department should examine the circumstances of the whole activity and consider all relevant evidence, avoiding mechanical application. Examples and case law (e.g., Flint Eng'g, Superior Care, Silk) emphasize that no single factor or subset of factors automatically dictates status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control (hiring party's right to control the manner and means)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate the hiring party's right to control how the work is performed — the manner and means by which the product is accomplished.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider contractual rights and practical supervision (scheduling, approval, discipline, review), and analyze this factor from the employer's perspective. Unexercised rights to supervise or control remain relevant (Superior Care). Right-to-control case law and Restatement authority inform the inquiry (Darden; Silk).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to work for others / exclusivity (practical ability to work for other employers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether the worker can, in practice, provide services for other employers or customers and whether contractual or operational constraints effectively preclude working for others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look beyond contractual language to how scheduling, monitoring systems, or policies (e.g., complex approval/monitoring of trips, deactivation policies, scheduling that makes other work impossible) operate in practice (Keller; Scantland; Brant; Razak). The ability to work for rivals or to transport personal clients can indicate less control and weigh toward independent contractor status (Paragon; Saleem).

rubrics_metrics.name: Opportunity for profit or loss / managerial skill
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider whether the worker has a realistic opportunity for profit or risk of loss from managerial or business decisions (e.g., selecting assignments, pricing, hiring helpers) that affects economic incentives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the worker can exercise managerial skill to increase profits (Brant example: hauling freight for other carriers relevant to ability to select favorable loads). The Department reintegrates managerial initiative into the skill/opportunity analysis and treats opportunity for profit or loss as probative of independent business status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skill and initiative (specialized skill and independent initiative)
rubrics_metrics.description: Examine the level of specialized skill required and whether the worker exercises initiative (marketing, setting price, business decisions) indicative of operating an independent business.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specialized skill alone does not conclusively indicate independent-contractor status (highly skilled workers can be employees and vice versa). Examples: driving generally is not a 'special skill' (Razak); landscapers may lack specialized skill yet be independent contractors if other factors (pricing, capital, multiple clients) show independence (department example). The Department rejects treating skill as a lower-weight 'core' factor and emphasizes initiative as part of skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investment in facilities and equipment
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess the extent of the worker's capital investment in facilities, tools, equipment, or other resources necessary to perform the work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Greater independent investment (beyond ordinary transportation or routine supplies) tends to indicate operation of an independent business; lesser investment suggests economic dependence on the employer. Examples and illustrative scenarios are used throughout the rulemaking to show how investment interacts with other factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permanency and duration of the relationship
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider whether the working relationship is of a permanent, long-term, or indefinite duration versus a temporary or project-based engagement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A long-standing, continuous relationship (especially when coupled with other indicia of control) weighs toward employee status, while short-term, project-based, or intermittent relationships may support independent-contractor status. Courts have found tenure and permanence probative but not dispositive (Faludi; other cases).

rubrics_metrics.name: Services are integral to the principal's business (integral part of the business)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate the degree to which the worker's services are a necessary or integral component of the alleged employer's business.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the worker performs the primary or essential work of the business (e.g., dancers for an exotic dance club, security guards for a security company), this tends to indicate employee status. However, integration into the business is one factor among many and is not conclusive (Silk; Off Duty Police; Superior Care; Lauritzen).

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether the worker is in business for themselves (independent business indicators)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess indicia that the worker is operating an independent business: marketing to multiple clients, setting prices, making business decisions, hiring helpers, and bearing financial risk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Workers who meaningfully control pricing, solicit customers, invest in an independent enterprise, and work for many clients are more likely to be independent contractors. The Department's landscaper example illustrates that lack of specialized skill can be offset by clear independent-business attributes (pricing, capital, multiple clients, non-integral services).

rubrics_metrics.name: Actual practices over formal contractual terms (substance over form)
rubrics_metrics.description: Look beyond how the parties label their relationship or what contracts state to the actual economic realities and day-to-day practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts and the Department examine what workers actually do, not merely what they could do hypothetically or what the contract says (Parrish; Saleem; Sureway). Stipulations of 'independent contractor' in agreements do not determine status when facts show otherwise (Safarian).

rubrics_metrics.name: Unexercised powers, rights, and freedoms are relevant
rubrics_metrics.description: An employer's reserved contractual rights (even if not exercised) to control or supervise the worker remain probative in the analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulatory text and case law emphasize that unexercised contractual rights can demonstrate control and weigh toward employee status; the Department endorses considering these unexercised rights as part of the control factor (87 FR discussion; Superior Care).

rubrics_metrics.name: Actual economic dependence (focus on economic reality rather than hypotheticals)
rubrics_metrics.description: The central inquiry is whether, as a matter of economic reality, workers are dependent upon the employer for work or are in business for themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess what workers actually did and whether they were economically dependent, not merely theoretical powers or possibilities. Courts caution against reliance on economic hypotheticals (Parrish; Saleem; Sureway).

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-exhaustive factors and no predetermined weighting (allow other relevant considerations)
rubrics_metrics.description: The list of factors is illustrative, not exhaustive; other relevant facts may inform the economic-dependence inquiry and the weight given to each factor depends on the case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department rejects the notion of fixed 'core' factors with predetermined weights (rejecting the 2021 IC Rule's core-factor approach). Agencies and courts should recognize additional factors raised by stakeholders and consider them where relevant, per case law (Sureway; Razak; Silk) and regulatory discussion (response to National Restaurant Association concerns).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid mechanical or checklist application (qualitative, contextual evaluation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid rigid or mechanical scoring; the inquiry is contextual and qualitative rather than a formulaic checklist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The analysis should synthesize how factors interact in practice; courts have repeatedly warned against giving dispositive effect to isolated facts or treating the factors as a checklist. Examples show courts resolving close factual questions by weighing multiple interacting factors (Flint Eng'g; Superior Care; numerous circuit opinions cited).
